claims.text: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloys have dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Adding a minor segregating dopant such as boron during processing will improve tensile strength.
Adding a minor segregating dopant such as boron during processing will improve room-temperature tensile ductility.
A minor boron addition can segregate to interfaces between the lamellar phases.
Suitable processing can preserve the lamellar-colony morphology while promoting dopant segregation without forming unwanted second phases.
The intervention will produce a thin segregated dopant layer, described as a complexion, at lamellar-colony boundaries.
The segregated dopant layer increases interfacial cohesion.
Enhanced interfacial bonding reduces local stress concentrations.
Enhanced interfacial bonding reduces microcrack nucleation.
Improved boundary cohesion enables better dislocation transmission.
Improved boundary cohesion enables greater work hardening.
Better dislocation transmission and work hardening simultaneously increase tensile strength and ductility.
The doped alloy will have measurably higher tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The doped alloy will have greater elongation to failure than the unmodified baseline at room temperature.
The conventional baseline exhibits early microcracking at poorly bonded internal boundaries.
Early boundary microcracking causes the conventional baseline to have limited ductility despite high strength.
The intervention is effective only if the dopant segregates to lamellar boundaries without forming deleterious phases.
The intervention may not apply to alloy systems in which dopant distribution cannot be controlled.
